---
title: "2. Implement and test a capsule"
subtitle: "Implement oe.greeting behind its contract with stdlib only; cover it with unit and contract tests, structured errors, and useful diagnostics."
---

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Implement one small capability behind its capsule contract, treating
  the capsule's `spec.inputs` and `spec.outputs` as the only public
  surface the implementation may rely on.
- Keep third-party dependencies local to the implementation (here,
  Python stdlib only) and explain where a non-stdlib dependency would
  live if the capability needed one.
- Write **unit tests** against the implementation and **contract
  tests** whose cases are derived at test time from the capsule
  document, so a drift between code and contract fails a test rather
  than ships silently.
- Handle a missing required input as a structured error — not a
  stack-trace crash — at the capability boundary.
- State what to log from a capsule implementation and why, without
  pulling in a logging framework.

These objectives map one-to-one to the five "Teach" bullets of
[`memo23.md`](../../../../memo23.md) §4 Module 3.

## Prerequisites

- Completed [Part 2 · Module 2 — Define a capsule](../01-define-a-capsule/index.qmd).
- A working shell and text editor.
- Python 3.8+ on `PATH`; `pyyaml` installed (for the contract test).
- No database, broker, AI library, bot platform, or Kubernetes.

::: {.callout-important title="Course-local call convention — not an upstream convention"}
This lesson calls the capsule as a plain Python function behind its
declared `spec.inputs`/`spec.outputs`. That calling shape is a
**course-local teaching harness only**. The implementation convention
for capsules belongs to `open-engineering-capsule/source` (the
implementation org, memo2 §1 D1), which has published none yet
([`memo24.md`](../../../../memo24.md) §2.1 as updated by observation
at upstream commit `bf071c2c1b57`).
When the implementation org publishes a convention, the Academy will
consume it; this course will not fork or shadow it
([`memo23.md`](../../../../memo23.md) §3.2,
[`memo26.md`](../../../../memo26.md) §5).
:::

## Implementing behind the contract

The capsule document authored in [Module 2](../01-define-a-capsule/index.qmd#a-valid-minimal-capsule)
declares the capability's **only** public surface: one input (`value`,
required, `string`) and one output (`greeting`, `string`). An
implementation satisfies the contract when it:

- reads only the declared inputs by their declared names and types;
- returns exactly the declared outputs by their declared names and
  types;
- fails loudly, in a structured way, when a declared-required input is
  absent.

The reference implementation at
[`labs/greeting-capsule/solution/greeting.py`](../../../../labs/greeting-capsule/solution/greeting.py)
does precisely this in Python stdlib:

```python
class MissingRequiredInput(Exception):
    """Raised when a declared-required capsule input is not provided."""

    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(f"missing required input: {name!r}")
        self.name = name


def greeting(inputs: dict) -> dict:
    if "value" not in inputs or inputs["value"] is None:
        raise MissingRequiredInput("value")
    value = inputs["value"]
    if not isinstance(value, str):
        raise TypeError(
            f"input 'value' must be a string per capsule.yaml, got {type(value).__name__}"
        )
    return {"greeting": f"Hello, {value}!"}
```

No capsule-visible state. No side effects. No module-level import
outside the standard library. A later implementation org convention
may wrap this function differently; it will not change what the
contract says.

## Keeping dependencies local

[`memo23.md`](../../../../memo23.md) §5 rules 2 (Optional by default)
and 3 (Explicit dependencies) say the Pico core must not inherit
every capability's library choices. The capsule-first corollary is:
whichever libraries a capsule implementation needs live **inside that
implementation**, declared in its own packaging manifest, and are
visible to a composing Pico only through the capsule's declared
contract (not as a transitive requirement on the core).

The `oe.greeting` capsule needs no third-party library at all; Python
stdlib suffices. The lab accordingly ships no `requirements.txt`
inside `solution/`. If a later capability needed, say, `httpx`, it
would be pinned in a sibling capsule implementation's manifest and
imported inside that implementation — never from `bin/pico` and never
from a sibling capsule.

## Unit tests vs contract tests

The lab ships two test modules under
[`labs/greeting-capsule/solution/tests/`](../../../../labs/greeting-capsule/solution/tests/):

| Module | What it asserts | What a failure means |
|---|---|---|
| [`test_greeting.py`](../../../../labs/greeting-capsule/solution/tests/test_greeting.py) | Specific behaviour of the Python function (e.g. `greeting({"value": "Pico"}) == {"greeting": "Hello, Pico!"}`). | The implementation stopped producing the expected concrete answer. |
| [`test_contract.py`](../../../../labs/greeting-capsule/solution/tests/test_contract.py) | Properties derived at test time from `solution/capsule.yaml` (capability identifier, each declared-required input raises `MissingRequiredInput` when absent, declared input/output names and types are honoured). | The implementation has drifted from the capsule contract, regardless of whether any one example still works. |

The split matters because it isolates two different reasons to fail.
A unit test can keep passing while the contract test catches a rename
or a type change in the capsule document, and vice versa. The
contract test does not re-encode the contract — it **reads** the
capsule document and derives the cases from it, so there is one
source of truth for the contract (`capsule.yaml`) and one source of
truth for the implementation (`greeting.py`).

Run both together, from inside `labs/greeting-capsule/`:

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s solution/tests
```

Expected tail: `Ran 8 tests in 0.001s` / `OK`.

## Error handling at the capability boundary

[`memo23.md`](../../../../memo23.md) §5 rule 9 (Graceful failure)
requires that missing capabilities and incompatible contracts are
reported clearly rather than silently falling back to unsafe or
unexpected behaviour. At the single-capsule level that means: a
declared-required input that is absent raises a **named**, catchable
exception that carries the missing input's name — not a generic
`KeyError` and not a stack trace from somewhere deep in the function.

The reference implementation uses `MissingRequiredInput("value")`.
The contract test iterates over every declared-required input in the
capsule document and asserts the exception's `.name` matches, so a
future capsule that adds a second required input will fail the test
until the implementation handles it the same way.

## Diagnostics without a framework

[`memo23.md`](../../../../memo23.md) §5 rule 10 (Observable
operation) asks for useful diagnostics without forcing every capsule
to adopt the same internal technology stack. For a stdlib function
this means logging to Python's standard `logging` module (not to a
chosen framework), at these points and no others:

- the capability identifier and capsule `metadata.version` once per
  process, at the first call, so a reader can tell **which** capsule
  implementation served the request;
- a structured record on each `MissingRequiredInput` with the input
  name, so an operator can tell *which* input was missing without
  reading the stack trace.

The lab's reference implementation does not add logging today
(stdlib-only, 44 lines); the [exercise](exercise.qmd) walks through
where and why it would go if you added it. A later Module 5 lesson
("Run and inspect the Pico") will cover log plumbing at the Pico
boundary.
